passages.t: Called by name, through water and fire
passages.happening:
The LORD who created and formed Jacob and Israel says, ‘Do not fear, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by your name; you are Mine’ (verse 1).

‘When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and when you go through the rivers, they will not overwhelm you. When you walk through the fire, you will not be scorched’ (verse 2). ‘For I am the LORD your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Savior; I give Egypt for your ransom, Cush and Seba in your place’ (verse 3). ‘Because you are precious and honored in My sight, and because I love you’ (verse 4), he will give peoples in exchange for them.

‘Do not be afraid, for I am with you’ (verse 5). He will gather their children from east and west, and tell the north to give them up and the south not to hold them back (verses 5-6), everyone called by his name and made for his glory (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
The chapter after the blind and deaf servant opens with no rebuke at all. God speaks to the same people as their maker and redeemer. To redeem was to buy back a relative from slavery or debt, and to call by name was to claim as one's own.

Waters and fire recall the crossing of the sea and the trials of the wilderness. God does not promise that they will not go through them, but that he will be with them in them.

The exiles were scattered in every direction, not only in Babylon. The promise to gather them from east, west, north and south pictures a homecoming for all of them, sons and daughters alike.
passages.later: Daniel's friends later walked through the furnace, and ‘the fire had no effect on the bodies of these men’ (Daniel 3:27). A psalm sings, ‘we went through fire and water, but You brought us into abundance’ (Psalm 66:12).
passages.hard:
How can God give other nations as a ransom for Israel? Does he value some peoples above others?

The line jars a modern reader, and it should be taken seriously. Most interpreters read it as poetry in the language of a ransom price: God would pay anything, even the greatest kingdoms of the day, to recover his people. It is a statement of how precious Israel is to him, not a policy of sacrificing others. Some also connect it with history: the Persian Empire, which released Israel, later conquered Egypt, as though Persia were given Egypt in exchange for letting Israel go.

The same chapters insist that the nations are invited into God's salvation (42:6; 45:22; 49:6), and that Israel was chosen to be a light to them. Israel's election is not favoritism but a calling. The book holds together God's particular love for his people and his intention to do good to every nation through them. Nothing in the verse gives anyone a reason to count any people as worth less than another.
passages.asks: God calls his people by name and says they are his, precious and loved. Ask whether you believe God speaks to you that way. And ask what waters and fires you are walking through now, and whether you know he is with you in them.

passages.happening:
‘Bring out a people who have eyes but are blind, and who have ears but are deaf’ (verse 8). Let the nations gather and bring their witnesses. Which of them foretold this (verse 9)?

‘You are My witnesses,’ declares the LORD, ‘and My servant whom I have chosen, so that you may consider and believe Me and understand that I am He’ (verse 10). Before him no god was formed, and none will come after.

‘I, yes I, am the LORD, and there is no Savior but Me’ (verse 11). He announced, saved and proclaimed, not some foreign god. ‘So you are My witnesses,’ declares the LORD, ‘that I am God’ (verse 12). ‘Even from eternity I am He, and none can deliver out of My hand. When I act, who can reverse it?’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The courtroom returns. The nations bring their witnesses for their gods. God brings his: Israel, the blind and deaf people of chapter 42. They are poor witnesses in themselves, but they are the ones who have seen what God foretold and did.

The chapter's great claim is that there is no Savior but the LORD. The exiles lived among many gods and saviors. They are told they exist to testify that only one God saves.
passages.later: The risen Jesus tells his followers, ‘you will be My witnesses’ (Acts 1:8). Moses sang, ‘See now that I am He; there is no God besides Me’ (Deuteronomy 32:39).
passages.asks: God calls blind and deaf people to be his witnesses. Ask what you have seen God do that you could testify to. And ask whether your weakness has kept you from speaking, when God chose witnesses who were weak.

passages.t: A new thing, a way in the wilderness
passages.happening:
‘Thus says the LORD your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel’ (verse 14): for their sake he will send to Babylon and bring down its fugitives, the Chaldeans in the ships they were proud of. He is their Holy One, their Creator and King (verse 15).

He is the LORD who made a way through the sea and a path through mighty waters, who drew out chariot and horse and army to lie down and never rise again, snuffed out like a wick (verses 16-17).

‘Do not call to mind the former things; pay no attention to the things of old’ (verse 18). ‘Behold, I am about to do something new; even now it is coming. Do you not see it? Indeed, I will make a way in the wilderness and streams in the desert’ (verse 19). Even the jackals and ostriches will honor him for the water he gives his chosen people (verse 20). ‘The people I formed for Myself will declare My praise’ (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Verses 16 and 17 describe the exodus from Egypt: the sea parted, Pharaoh's chariots drowned. Then, surprisingly, God says to forget the former things. Not because the exodus did not matter, but because what he is about to do will be greater: a new exodus, from Babylon, with a way through the desert and rivers in the wasteland.

The first hearers had lived on memories of what God had once done. They were told to look up and see the new thing already springing up.
passages.later: Paul writes, ‘if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away. Behold, the new has come’ (2 Corinthians 5:17). And God says at the end of the Bible, ‘Behold, I make all things new’ (Revelation 21:5).
passages.asks: God tells his people not to dwell on the past, because he is doing something new. Ask what past, good or bad, you are dwelling on. And ask whether you can see the new thing God may be beginning.

passages.t: Sins that burden God, and sins blotted out
passages.happening:
‘But you have not called on Me, O Jacob, because you have grown weary of Me, O Israel’ (verse 22). They did not bring him their sheep or honor him with sacrifices; he did not burden them with offerings (verse 23). ‘But you have burdened Me with your sins; you have wearied Me with your iniquities’ (verse 24).

‘I, yes I, am He who blots out your transgressions for My own sake and remembers your sins no more’ (verse 25).

Remind him, he says; let them argue the case and state it if they can be found right (verse 26). Their first father sinned, and their spokesmen rebelled (verse 27). So he disgraced the leaders of the sanctuary and gave Jacob over to destruction and Israel to scorn (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
The reversal is sharp. God had not burdened his people with demands, but they had burdened him with their sins. They had grown tired of God, when it was God who should have been tired of them.

And then the center of the passage: God blots out their sins, for his own sake, and remembers them no more. Not because they deserve it. Because of who he is.

The first father who sinned is not named. Israel's sin goes back to its beginnings. The judgment of verse 28 is the exile itself, now looked back on. The promise of verse 25 stands in the middle of it.
passages.later: Jeremiah hears the same promise in the new covenant: ‘For I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more’ (Jeremiah 31:34), and Hebrews quotes it (Hebrews 8:12). A psalm says, ‘As far as the east is from the west, so far has He removed our transgressions from us’ (Psalm 103:12).
passages.asks: God says he blots out sins for his own sake. Ask whether you believe your forgiveness rests on who God is rather than on how well you have done. And ask whether you have grown weary of God, when he has not grown weary of you.
